title: Idols from the House
hookLine: the idols are removed from the Ka'ba as he recites, truth has come and falsehood vanished (17:81)

cards: Three hundred and sixty idols stand around the Ka'ba on the day of the conquest, Sahih al-Bukhari says. Stone and wood, gods of many names.
The house itself is plain stone in a valley, which the Qur'an says Abraham and his son Ishmael raised for the worship of the one God. For generations, pilgrims had come here and prayed to the idols.
Now the Prophet ﷺ walks up to them with a stick in his hand. Nobody fights him. Nobody stops him.
He's reciting something as he goes, and the words are older than this morning.

teach.b: Sahih al-Bukhari records the scene. As he went round the idols, he pointed at them with the stick, or struck them, and they fell, and he recited a verse from the seventeenth surah.
In Pickthall's old translation: "Truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away. Lo! falsehood is ever bound to vanish." It doesn't say truth fought falsehood and won after a long war.
Truth came, and falsehood simply went. Like turning on a light: you don't have to drag the dark out of the room. Muslims read the clearing of the Ka'ba as a return, not a new building.
In their telling, the house was always meant for one God, and the idols were add-ons, piled up over time, so removing them gave the house back to what it was for.
The reports add a detail: images inside the Ka'ba were removed too, and he would not enter until they were. And notice what did not happen.
The people who had prayed to those idols were the same people he set free that same day. The statues came down; the people were let go.

teach.h: FIRM WITH THE IDOL, GENTLE WITH THE PERSON.
teach.b: Muslim teachers often hold those two side by side: firm about the false thing, gentle with the person who held it.
That's a hard balance in any family argument. And the verse's last line, falsehood is ever bound to vanish, Muslims read as a rule, not a single morning.

how: Muslims recite 17:81 when speaking of the conquest of Mecca and the clearing of the Ka'ba, and teachers use the scene to explain tawhid: the house restored to the worship of one God.

games.q: you're standing before the Ka'ba with three hundred and sixty idols around it and a stick in your hand. what do you say?
o: a speech against the tribes who made them.
a verse: truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away.
games.why: al-Bukhari records that he recited 17:81 as each one fell. no speech against anyone, just the verse.

practice: Look around the room you're in for one thing that tells you a lie: a mirror you only use to criticize yourself, a screen that promises rest and never gives it, a note that says you're not enough.
Just notice it, and decide what you'll do with it. If you pray, you can recite the verse quietly, as he recited it, truth has come; if you don't, sit with the room a little clearer.

wordCard.voice: Al-Haqq, the Truth, one of the names of God: the word recited over every fallen statue the day the Ka'ba was cleared.

orig.note: Arabic: truth has come. al-haqq is also one of the names of God: the Real, the True.

carryVoice: Your line: truth has come. It came, and the dark simply went. See you tomorrow.
